title: The Hundred Years' War: Longbows, Plague and Joan of Arc

cards.b:
From 1337 to 1453 England and France fought on and off over the French crown, land and trade. The war is famous for longbows, knights, the Black Death and a teenage girl who led an army.

It also helped to shape the idea of England and France as nations, with their own kings, taxes and armies. Many of the battles were small. The war's effects were huge.

In 1337 Edward III of England claimed the French crown through his mother, Isabella, sister of the last French king. Philip VI of France was already on the throne, and the French would not accept an English king.

Other disputes made things worse. The duchy of Gascony was English land in France, and the wool trade of Flanders tied the economies of the two countries together. Each side wanted control of the other.

At Crécy in 1346 English archers with longbows shot down French knights and crossbowmen. At Poitiers in 1356 the French king John II was captured. The battles changed how Europeans saw the knight.

Henry V's victory at Agincourt in 1415 was even more dramatic. The French army was far larger, but it got stuck in the mud, and thousands of French nobles were killed or captured.

Jean Froissart (c. 1337–c. 1405)

A poet and chronicler from the county of Hainaut, Froissart wrote a huge account of the wars. He loved knightly courage and the grand style of battles.

He wrote for rich patrons, so his story favours the nobles. Read him for the feel of the age, and check him against other sources for the facts.
The war did not run without a break. It was a series of campaigns, truces and sieges across France.

Joan of Arc was a young peasant woman from Domrémy who said she heard voices of saints. In 1429 she joined the French army and helped lift the English siege of Orléans. Soon after, the Dauphin was crowned as Charles VII at Reims.

Joan was captured in 1430. An English-backed court tried her and had her burned at Rouen in 1431. In 1456 a new court declared her trial unjust, and she is now a saint of the Catholic Church.

cards.h: A war that lasted a hundred years?
cards.b:
The name "Hundred Years' War" suggests one long, unbroken fight. The picture is useful for school lessons, but it is misleading.

Historians point out that there were long truces, quiet decades and sudden bursts of fighting. The name came later, and the war was made up of many separate conflicts. Historians argue about the best way to divide them into phases.

cards.h: The Black Death and the peasants
cards.b:
The Black Death arrived in England in 1348. It killed perhaps a third to a half of the population across Europe, which led to labour shortages and higher wages. Armies struggled to find men.

In 1381 English peasants rose in revolt over poll taxes and the harsh rules of serfdom. The rebellion was crushed, but it showed how the war, the plague and taxes were tied together.

To pay for the war, kings raised taxes and borrowed money. In France, Charles VII created permanent companies of soldiers in the 1440s, one of the earliest standing armies in Europe.

Historians argue that the war helped build modern states. Taxes, professional armies and national feeling grew stronger, though the process took centuries. The English language also gained ground at court and in law.

The war effectively ended in 1453 at the battle of Castillon in Gascony. The French artillery, using large cannon, defeated the English army led by John Talbot, who was killed.

England kept only Calais. The loss of Gascony ended more than three hundred years of English rule in southwestern France. English kings would still claim the French crown for centuries, but the war was over.

While England and France fought, the Delhi Sultanate in India was expanding fast. Alauddin Khalji, who ruled from 1296 to 1316, pushed his armies deep into the Deccan and the far south.

In 1311 his general Malik Kafur raided the Pandya city of Madurai. Such raids brought loot and tribute to Delhi. They also show a parallel: two great powers on opposite ends of Eurasia were running wars of plunder and state-building in the same century.

Five things to remember
  1. The war ran from 1337 to 1453.
  2. Crécy (1346), Poitiers (1356) and Agincourt (1415) were key English victories.
  3. Joan of Arc relieved Orléans in 1429 and was burned in 1431.
  4. The Black Death struck in 1348.
  5. The war ended at Castillon in 1453, with French artillery.
Think about it
  • Did longbows change war more than knights did?
  • Did the war build nations, or did it just drain money?
